\# Pattern Record: Carbon-Aware Workload Scheduling \*\*Category:\*\* Sustainable Infrastructure / Operational Efficiencies\\ \*\*Status:\*\* Draft # # Context Organizations joyfully on compute-intensive workloads such as analytics pipelines, machine learning training, or large batch jobs. These are often run at fixed times for historical or operational convenience, without regard for when the electricity grid is cleaner or dirtier. Because energy mix changes throughout the day and across regions, this practice can significantly increase the carbon footprint of IT. # # Problem The challenge is how to reduce the environmental impact of heavy workloads without compromising business value. Most teams lack visibility into the real-time carbon intensity of the energy grid. Even if that data is available, business deadlines, costs, and operational predictability all create pressure to keep running jobs exactly as before. # # Forces There are competing priorities at play: - Sustainability goals call for shifting work to low-carbon hours. - Service agreements demand timeliness and predictability. - Cloud pricing adds financial complexity, sometimes reinforcing but other times conflicting with carbon goals. - Multi-region systems face different carbon profiles depending on location. # # Solution A carbon-aware scheduler incorporates grid carbon-intensity data into workload orchestration. Jobs are classified into flexible and critical categories. Flexible workloads—such as data transformations, nightly reports, or rendering tasks—can be delayed or shifted to times when cleaner energy is available. Critical services remain fixed but are still monitored for visibility. Scheduling policies balance deadlines with sustainability: a workload may run immediately if a deadline is close, but otherwise it will wait for a lower-carbon window. Cloud provider or third-party APIs supply the real-time carbon data needed. Results are monitored so that architects can demonstrate both emission savings and business impact. # # Resulting Context When applied consistently, this pattern leads to measurable reductions in operational emissions. It builds awareness of the carbon footprint of IT across teams and often aligns with cost savings where low-carbon hours also coincide with lower energy pricing. The trade-off is additional complexity in orchestration systems and the need for business stakeholders to accept some variability in processing times.![graph%20TB%0Aa--%3Eb](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)\# # Consequences \*\*Benefits:\*\* tangible reductions in carbon impact, improved ESG reporting, and a visible demonstration of sustainable IT practices.\\ \*\*Liabilities:\*\* more complex scheduling systems, the need for cultural change around flexible workload timing, and occasional conflicts with strict deadlines. # # Related Patterns - Selecting greener data center regions - Classifying workloads by sustainability flexibility - Managing lifecycle debt through intentional decommissioning # # Known Uses Google has implemented “carbon-intelligent computing” to shift jobs based on grid signals. Microsoft provides APIs to support similar approaches, and financial institutions have piloted this practice to meet sustainability targets. ## # \*\*Experimentation\*\* This technique requires additional experimentation to determine behavior, applicable environments and beneficial measures. # # BTABoK Connections This pattern strengthens the \*\*sustainability quality attribute\*\*, while interacting with performance and cost attributes. It demonstrates the “Doing Good” and “Financial” value dimensions, integrating sustainability into planning, transformation, and measurement stages of the architecture lifecycle. # Pattern Record: Carbon-Aware Workload Scheduling \*\*Category:\*\* Sustainable Infrastructure / Operational Efficiency\\ \*\*Status:\*\* Draft # # Context Organizations increasingly rely on compute-intensive workloads such as analytics pipelines, machine learning training, or large batch jobs.
